newsitem.title: UK: GOLF-SCOTTISH HOLDERS UPSET BY SWEDEN IN DUNHILL CUP.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-SCOTTISH HOLDERS UPSET BY SWEDEN IN DUNHILL CUP.

text.p: World number two Colin Montgomerie lost his match as holders Scotland were shocked 2-1 by a Swedish team missing their two best players in the Alfred Dunhill Cup on Thursday.

Zimbabwe, the team beaten by Scotland in last year's final, also had a fight on their hands before escaping with a 2-1 victory over 1,000-1 outsiders India in their opening round robin group match in the same section.

Meanwhile, American Mark O'Meara fired eight successive birdies from the second hole of the Old Course as he played the front nine in 28 and looked certain to threaten the course record of 62 set by compatriot Curtis Strange in the 1987 event. O'Meara still had the back nine to play.
Montgomerie, who on Sunday clinched his record-tying fourth successive European Order of Merit title, was beaten 68 to 69 by Jarmo Sandelin despite shooting birdies at the first three holes.
That was the decisive match after Andrew Coltart won for the fifth-seeded Scots 67-70 against Peter Hedblom and Patrick Sjoland levelled for Sweden with a 68-69 triumph over Raymond Russell.
"Now we need to win our next two ties 3-0 and hope the Swedes lose one," Montgomerie said.
He said his match turned at the 16th, where Sandelin's second shot appeared to be going out of bounds.
"It stayed in by a foot and he holed a putt from 110 feet for a birdie. It looked as if he was going to bogey the hole but instead I made par and lost it."

Sweden, who won the title in 1991, are without two of their best players, Lancome Trophy champion Jesper Parnevik, who has stopped playing for the year, and Ryder Cup player Per Ulrik Johansson, whose victory in the European Open last month came too late to qualify him for this team.

Montgomerie almost sank his approach at the first hole when his shot spun back and just missed hitting the flag. He made his four-footer for a birdie and Sandelin could only make par after his approach spun back to the edge of the Swilcan Burn, the stream which fronts the green.
The Scot birdied the next two and Sandelin admitted afterwards that he was a bit worried.
"But I've learned that if you find your own game and focus on making the putts you can recover," he said.
Two behind at the turn, he birdied the 11th and 12th and his huge putt at 16th clinched the victory.

India, playing the prestigious one million pounds sterling ($1.56 million) event for the first time, ran the fourth-seeded Zimbabwean trio surprisingly close considering their relative lack of experience.

Ali Sher beat Tony Johnstone 72-73 in the first match but Mark McNulty squared the tie with a 70-73 win over Asian Masters champion Gaurav Ghei, who double-bogeyed the "Road Hole" 17th after hitting the infamous greenside bunker.
Former world number one Nick Price then sewed it up for Zimbabwe with a 70-71 victory over Jeev Singh, helped by three birdies on the first six holes of the back nine.
"We knew at the start of the day that there are no easy games anymore," Johnstone said.
Ghei was disappointed with his performance, particularly the blow-out at the 17th.
"We had a good chance of causing a major surprise. But there is no reason why we should lose heart," he said.
Third seeds South Africa had a 2-1 win over 1994 champions Canada, with world number four Ernie Els shooting a seven-under-par 65 to beat Rick Gibson by eight strokes.
Wayne Westner crushed Rick Todd 68-77 while Jim Rutledge gave Canada some consolation with a 69-76 win over Retief Goosen.
